PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 12, audited at commit 080ce1e (committed, HEAD of the main
checkout, so the recorded tree hash fd1ea1f7... is the audited content -- the Sprint
11 mismatch does not recur here). Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this
verdict. Ten files, all under lib/ephemeris/, no UI, as required.

VERDICT: PASS.

R10 IS THE CRITERION EVERYTHING RESTS ON, so I did not settle for a green suite. The
test file claims its expected orbs were derived in Python from raw JPL Horizons
longitudes rather than by running this module. That claim is checkable, because
Sprint 6 already put those longitudes on the record and I verified them then. I
re-derived all ten reference orbs arithmetically from Sprint 6's audited longitudes:

  1850-01-01  Uranus-Pluto conj      claimed 4.5878  derived 4.5878
  1850-01-01  Sun-Mercury conj       claimed 7.4257  derived 7.4257
  1850-01-01  Venus-Mars opp         claimed 4.1557  derived 4.1557
  1850-01-01  Mercury-Jupiter trine  claimed 5.2922  derived 5.2922
  1950-06-15  Sun-Moon conj          claimed 7.3875  derived 7.3875
  1950-06-15  Neptune-Pluto sextile  claimed 1.6637  derived 1.6637
  1950-06-15  Jupiter-Saturn opp     claimed 6.1563  derived 6.1563
  2024-03-20  Sun-Neptune conj       claimed 2.8937  derived 2.8937
  2024-03-20  Venus-Saturn conj      claimed 1.6393  derived 1.6393
  2024-03-20  Jupiter-Uranus conj    claimed 5.3090  derived 5.3090

Worst deviation 0.000044 degrees. Every value is reproducible with a circular
distance and a subtraction from data this project independently verified two sprints
ago. The reference set is real, it is not this module's own output laundered back in
as a test, and anyone can redo the arithmetic.

Requirements coverage:
R1 MET, exactly. conjunction 0/8, opposition 180/8, trine 120/7, square 90/7,
  sextile 60/4 -- checked character by character against the handoff's own table
  (docs/design/HANDOFF_chart_constellation.md). Nothing rounded, nothing adjusted.
R2 MET. `break` after the first match, and `.sort((x, y) => x.orb - y.orb)` in the
  module rather than left to the caller, with a test asserting monotonic orbs and
  another asserting one aspect per pair. The comment noting that the ranges do not
  actually overlap at these values is correct -- I checked: conjunction spans
  separation [0,8], sextile [56,64], square [83,97], trine [113,127], opposition
  [172,180]. So "first match" is a well-defined rule rather than a hidden tie-break.
R3 MET. `applying: orbLater < orbNow`, where the later separation is recomputed from
  both bodies' real later longitudes. This is body-agnostic by construction: it asks
  whether the orb is closing, which is the definition, rather than keying on which
  body is nominally faster. The retrograde case R3 names is covered by a real
  reference case (Uranus-Pluto 1850 with Pluto retrograde) plus a test that
  separately asserts Pluto actually is retrograde at that instant, so the case cannot
  silently stop being the case it was chosen for. See note 1 for the accuracy of the
  lookahead, which is a different question from the rule.
R4 MET. tightness = 1 - orb/maxOrb, exposed as a field, asserted by test. Grepped the
  whole diff for strokeWidth, stroke-width, opacity and oklch: zero hits in lib/ or
  app/. Sprint 13's rendering has not arrived early.
R5 MET. Element and modality maps cover all twelve signs, and a test asserts twelve
  fixtures sum to twelve, so a missing or duplicated sign fails rather than silently
  undercounting.
R6 MET, exactly. Bands match the handoff verbatim, including the narrow cardinals,
  and the test checks every boundary from both sides (9.999/10, 79.999/80, 99.999/100,
  169.999/170, 189.999/190, 259.999/260, 279.999/280, 349.999/350). All eight names
  covered. Boundary-from-both-sides is the difference between testing a band table
  and testing that a band table exists.
R7 MET. julianDay is exact rather than approximate, and the tests check it three ways:
  the Unix epoch, J2000 asserted with toBe rather than toBeCloseTo, and the handoff's
  own displayed reference (1986-04-26T01:23Z -> JD 2446546.5576). Using the design
  document's own printed number as a test fixture is a good instinct -- it ties the
  code to the artifact it has to agree with.
R8 MET. instantFromDateAndTime carries the same round-trip validation Sprint 6
  established, extended to hours and minutes, and the comment identifies the specific
  trap: "24:00" is valid ISO 8601 and JS silently rolls it to 00:00 the next day. The
  round trip catches it. That is the same class of thinking that caught 2024-02-30 in
  Sprint 6.
R9 MET, verified by tracing the import graph rather than by grepping for a string.
  Every import in lib/ephemeris/ (excluding tests) is: astronomy-engine, ./zodiac,
  ./adapter. No node: import, no server-only, no filesystem, no network anywhere in
  the reachable graph. The node: hits elsewhere in the repo (app/chart/actions.ts,
  the guardrail modules, app/api/health/db) are pre-existing and unreachable from
  these modules.
R10 MET. See above, plus: an absent-aspect case (Sun-Moon on 2024-03-20 correctly
  yields nothing), an applying case, a separating case, and the retrograde case.

Verified by execution:
- lint, typecheck, test: all exit 0. 110 tests across 11 files, up from 70.
- next build exits 0; route table unchanged -- /_not-found, /api/health/db, /chart,
  /reading/[id]. No UI shipped, which is R-zero for this sprint.
- Rebuilt with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="QA1PROBESERVICEROLE" and grepped all of
  .next: absent from the entire build output.

Notes, not conditions:
1. THE ONE WORTH ESCALATING, and it is about the design, not this diff. The
   applying/separating verdict is a finite difference over whatever step the caller
   passes as positionsLater. Every test here uses one day. I measured what that costs:
   over 365 daily instants through 2024, comparing a one-day lookahead against a
   one-hour one across 4,588 aspect instances --
     disagreements involving the Moon:      392
     disagreements not involving the Moon:  104
   Roughly one verdict in nine flips. Examples: 2024-01-01 Moon-Sun trine orb 4.046
   reads separating at one day and applying at one hour; 2024-01-04 Moon-Sun square
   orb 1.599, same disagreement. The cause is arithmetic, not a coding error: the
   Moon moves about 13 degrees a day against a maximum orb of 8, so a one-day
   lookahead can sail past exact and back out, and the shorter step is much closer to
   the instantaneous derivative that "applying" actually means.
   This is NOT a deviation from spec. I checked the prototype: line 333 of
   docs/design/prototype_chart_constellation.html is
   `const now = lonAt(jd), soon = lonAt(jd + 1);` and line 374 computes applying the
   same way this module does. Sprint 12 reproduced the reference implementation
   faithfully, which is why it passes -- R3 asks for both bodies' motion and that is
   exactly what it got.
   But Sprint 13 renders this as ` · A` / ` · S` on every aspect table row, and the
   sprint file's own risk register names "wrong output that looks plausible" as the
   thing to fear. The fix costs nothing and needs no change here: computeAspects takes
   positionsLater as an argument rather than choosing a step itself, so Sprint 13 can
   pass t+1h for the aspect call while keeping t+1day for retrograde detection, where
   a one-day step is appropriate. Worth a decision by whoever owns the design before
   Sprint 13 renders it, rather than after.
2. Following from note 1: computeAspects has no default and no stated step, so
   "positionsLater" is a contract carried entirely in a doc comment. Its own comment
   points at RETROGRADE_STEP_DAYS as "the convention used elsewhere in this
   codebase", which is the step note 1 shows is the imprecise one for this purpose.
   If Sprint 13 settles on a step, consider naming it in this module as an exported
   constant so the choice is visible at the call site rather than inferred.
3. countElements and countModalities count whatever they are given; nothing enforces
   ten bodies. Harmless -- every caller passes computePositions' output -- and the
   "twelve fixtures sum to twelve" test would not exist if the function were
   hard-coded to ten. Noting it only because R5 says "across the ten bodies" and the
   function does not say that anywhere.
4. The sprint file records GroundTruth's gate as deliberately thin and says a PASS
   there should not be read as evidence the aspect maths was exercised live. That is
   correct and I want it doubled here: this verdict is the verification for this
   sprint. Nothing downstream will exercise these numbers until Sprint 13 puts them
   on a page, and at that point they will be checked by eye against a rendering, which
   is exactly the unfalsifiable-by-inspection problem the sprint was built to avoid.

Cleared to ship at 080ce1e. Standing note for Pipeman: files under docs/sprints/ are
tracked and the tree is dirty with sprint bookkeeping -- do not fold any of it into
the shipped commit, the tree content is what /sprint-ship compares against this
verdict.

PASS: GroundTruth live test, Sprint 12, commit
080ce1efcc2f380a0365b4531ca6da67c8c030ca.
Environment: https://my-little-racoon.vercel.app, 2026-08-16 ~20:35Z.

VERDICT: PASS -- on a deliberately thin gate, exactly as the sprint file scopes it.

READ THIS BEFORE READING THE PASS. The sprint file states plainly that this sprint
ships no user-visible change, that the live gate is regression only, and that "a
PASS should not be read as evidence the aspect maths was exercised live." That is
correct and I am reinforcing it rather than softening it.

WHAT I DID NOT TEST, and could not: the five Ptolemaic aspects and their orb
table, first-match-only selection, ascending-orb sort, applying versus separating
from both bodies' relative motion (R3's retrograde-slower-body case especially),
the tightness value, element and modality counts, moon phase and its cardinal
bands, Julian Day, and positions at an arbitrary instant. None of it is reachable
from outside the running product. I confirmed that directly rather than assuming
it -- see the reachability check below. QA1's reference-chart audit is the only
gate this sprint's actual content has passed, and this PASS adds nothing to it.

REACHABILITY CHECK -- confirming there is genuinely nothing live to test.
  - Aspect vocabulary in the served /chart HTML (conjunction, opposition, trine,
    sextile, applying, separating, moon phase, waxing): 0 occurrences.
  - R8 extends positions to accept date AND time. That capability is NOT exposed
    in the UI. The only date control is
    <input id="date" type="date" min="1700-01-01" max="2100-12-31" required
    name="date"> -- no time input. And a time is ignored if supplied by hand:
      /chart?date=2024-03-20              -> Moon Leo 8.29, instant 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z
      /chart?date=2024-03-20&time=00:00   -> Moon Leo 8.29, instant 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z
      /chart?date=2024-03-20&time=23:59   -> Moon Leo 8.29, instant 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z
      /chart?date=2024-03-20T23:59        -> rejected: "2024-03-20T23:59" is not a
                                             date in YYYY-MM-DD form.
    The Moon does not move between those requests, and the page still states the
    fixed 12:00 UTC instant. R8's arbitrary-instant support is library-level only,
    which is consistent with the sprint's claim of no user-visible change. Worth
    noting for whoever builds Sprint 13: the surface is unchanged, so R8 is
    entirely unproven from outside and its first live exercise will be there.

REGRESSION CHECKS -- all clean.

1. /api/health/db reports the shipped commit. PASS.
   {"status":"ok","connected":true,
    "migrationVersion":"20260816181929_readings_positions_not_null",
    "commit":{"sha":"080ce1efcc2f380a0365b4531ca6da67c8c030ca",
              "short":"080ce1e","isLocal":false}}
   sha matches Pipeman's ship and origin/main exactly, all 40 characters. The
   Sprint 11 observable survived its first sprint of use, which is the thing every
   later live test depends on.

2. /chart still serves, and positions are unchanged. PASS, and this is the
   regression that actually mattered.
   Sprint 12 refactored the positions module (R8, arbitrary instant), so a silent
   numeric drift was the realistic failure mode. /chart?date=2024-03-20 returns:
     Sun Aries 0.37 | Moon Leo 8.29 | Mercury Aries 17.97 | Venus Pisces 10.63 |
     Mars Aquarius 28.06 | Jupiter Taurus 14.96 | Saturn Pisces 12.27 |
     Uranus Taurus 20.27 | Neptune Pisces 27.48 | Pluto Aquarius 1.67
   Byte-identical to the values I recorded in Sprint 6 and verified there against
   NASA JPL Horizons to within 20.4 arcsec. Every retrograde flag still No. The
   instant is still stated: 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z. The refactor moved no
   numbers.

3. Sprint 11's root redirect. PASS. GET / -> 307, location: /chart.

4. Sprint 10's save/retrieve. PASS. The reading saved during Sprint 10's test,
   59fbb41d-82a4-4786-83eb-17924d654718, still resolves: HTTP 200, "Reading for
   1969-07-20", Sun Cancer 27.58, Moon Libra 3.50, unchanged. I re-opened the
   existing reading rather than saving a new one, deliberately: anon cannot delete,
   so every save-path test permanently adds a production row, and this sprint's
   criteria did not require exercising the write path.

5. Sprint 10's negative guarantees. PASS. A freshly generated random reading id
   returns 404; /readings and /api/readings both return 404. No listing route has
   reappeared.

SUMMARY OF WHAT THIS PASS MEANS. The deployment carrying the aspect engine is live
at the right commit, and nothing it touched broke anything already proven: the
positions are numerically identical to JPL-verified values, the deployment
observable works, the redirect works, and saved readings still resolve. That is
the whole claim. The aspect engine itself remains verified only by QA1's static
reference-chart checking, and it stays that way until Sprint 13 puts it on screen.

TOOLING CAVEAT: no Playwright MCP or Chrome extension in this session. All checks
are curl over HTTPS against production. No browser rendering was observed and I am
not claiming any.
